title: The Dobrovoljacka Street Column
sources: Burg & Shoup, The War in Bosnia-Herzegovina (1999), Chapter 4 on the siege of Sarajevo
ICTY Karadzic Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T), context on JNA withdrawal
ICTY Galic Trial Judgment (IT-98-29-T), Sarajevo siege background
Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. I, JNA withdrawal from Sarajevo
content:
On the afternoon of 3 May 1992, a Yugoslav People's Army convoy attempting to withdraw from the Bistrik barracks in central Sarajevo was attacked along Dobrovoljačka street by Bosnian government forces. The incident — known to Serb sources as the Dobrovoljačka column massacre and to Bosnian government sources as the legitimate interception of an armed enemy column — produced a contested factual record that has remained one of the most disputed episodes of the early war.

The context was the formal withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnian territory. On 4 May 1992, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia announced that the JNA would withdraw from Bosnia, with the operation to be completed within fifteen days. In the days preceding the announcement, individual JNA units in Sarajevo had begun to evacuate barracks under arrangements negotiated with the Bosnian government and the United Nations Protection Force, which had a presence in the city. The Bistrik barracks evacuation on 2-3 May was one of these arrangements: a column of approximately two hundred and sixty soldiers, including the commander of the JNA Second Military District General Milutin Kukanjac, was to depart the barracks under UNPROFOR escort and proceed through the city to a location from which they could be evacuated.

What followed has been reconstructed from witness statements that diverge on key points. The convoy departed the barracks in the afternoon of 3 May with UNPROFOR vehicles at its head and tail. As the convoy moved along Dobrovoljačka street, it came under fire from positions held by Bosnian government forces. The fire continued for an extended period; by the time it ceased, between six and forty-two JNA soldiers were dead, depending on the source of the count, and a number of others were taken prisoner.

The Bosnian government's account of the events held that the convoy was carrying weapons, equipment, and intelligence officers in addition to the personnel agreed in the withdrawal arrangement; that the column had violated the terms of the safe passage; that the Territorial Defence units that engaged the column did so on those grounds; and that the casualties were, regrettably, the consequence of fighting in a chaotic urban environment with mixed civilian presence. The Bosnian Serb and Federal Republic accounts held that the column had been clearly identified, that it was being escorted by UNPROFOR, that the agreement had not authorised its interception, and that the fire on the column was a deliberate ambush of soldiers who were complying with a withdrawal arrangement.

The ICTY did not produce a chamber-level finding on the Dobrovoljačka incident comparable to its findings on Sarajevo siege incidents within its temporal jurisdiction. The Karadžić chamber referenced the period of JNA withdrawal as part of the context for the establishment of the VRS, but did not adjudicate the Dobrovoljačka events as a separate matter. Burg and Shoup, treating the incident in their broader account of the siege, characterised it as one of several episodes of the early war in which the chaos of the transition between JNA presence and Bosnian Serb military formation produced contested events with significant subsequent political resonance.

The political afterlife of the incident has been substantial. Investigations and prosecutions have been initiated by Serbian and, at various points, Bosnian Serb judicial authorities, with attempts to extradite Bosnian government officials whom they characterise as responsible. Bosnian government and Federation authorities have rejected those characterisations. The street itself, in the centre of Sarajevo, remains an ordinary urban thoroughfare; a memorial plaque to the JNA dead was placed and subsequently removed; political controversy over commemoration of the events has continued to recur.

The Dobrovoljačka incident occupies a distinctive position in the historical record of the Bosnian war: an early-war event whose contested factual basis has not been resolved by tribunal judgment, whose political afterlife has shaped post-war Serbian-Bosniak relations, and whose place in the war's narrative depends substantially on the perspective from which it is recounted.
